subject: can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
Hi!

I have encountered the bizarre situation that with increasing the sample size of my fake data simulation the computation time explodes discontinuously at some point and convergence of the parameter estimates vanishes suddenly.

I am simulating a number of patients using an ODE and then try to recover the parameters. I do so in a very simple way in that there is no between-subject variability and I provide Stan with a lot of data. What happens is when I run this with 4 or 6 patients, then everything is fine (running time is 61s and 75s / estimates are as simulated). Once I go to 8 patients then the running time explodes to 2h and the estimates are just crap.

From my rough understanding the limited precision of the ODE integrator (set to 1E-10, maybe in reality 1E-7) is the problem here. That is, I provide so much data that the MC error is below the 1E-7 which effectively renders the HMC sampler blind given the precision the data likelihood would provide. So I endup in the bizarre situation that more data kills my Stan run due to the limited ODE precision. What can be done about this? The obvious answer is to increase the ODE precision, but that is a limited game. Can we somehow force Stan to run the sampler with a limited precision? I mean, I don't mind in this situation iof the answer from the sampler is not as precise as the data would allow me to make inferences. However, I would really appreciate an answer in such a situation, but with an artificially more unprecise result - that would be much better than no answer at all.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
MCMC error is estimated as

posterior std-dev / sqrt(n_eff)

It's not something that gets controlled directly. Or are you
talking about the Hamiltonian simulation error due to the leapfrog
error? I think that's usually minimal until you hit a divergence and
it spins off to infinity.

It still gets through as many iterations in the 2H? Any idea if
you're spiking memory or something and starting to swap? Oare
are you seeing the tree depth explode?

Each of those integrate_ode calls is for an independent patient?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
Hi Bob!

Thanks for you answer. You are right in that I was actually referring to posterior std-dev and not MC error.

So I have J patients for which I integrate an ODE. All patients have the exact same parameter set.

For J=6 the posterior std-dev of the parameter of interest is of the order of 1E-2 and the usual sampler parameters look fine:

> sp6 <- get_sampler_params(res[["6"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> colMeans(sp6)
accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__ 
   0.90502219    0.02050799    3.60000000   18.52000000    0.00000000 
     energy__ 
 407.13425909 

Now, when I go to J=8, then I run the same number of iterations, yes (75 warmup and 50 post-warmup), but now things break seriously. The run takes 2H, nothing converges at all and the posterior sd is of the order of 1E-12! The sampler did go completely insane:

> sp8 <- get_sampler_params(res[["8"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> colMeans(sp8)
accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__ 
 1.001197e-01  5.093111e-16  1.000000e+01  1.023000e+03  0.000000e+00 
     energy__ 
 1.230724e+03 

So the stepsize got reduced to essentially 0, the treedepth is maxed out and we take 1023 leapfrog steps on average.

I think the reason is the limited accuracy of the ODE integrator here which somehow defeats NUTS. I do find this somewhat worrysome, as I thought that a robust numerical procedure should be able to cope with limited precision and simply output a result with limited precision. Anything else I can look into which helps?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
I don’t know what you expect NUTS, or any algorithm, to do.
When the ODE solver starts returning inaccurate gradients
then the Hamiltonian transitions are poor and the acceptance
probability plummets.  All NUTS can do is reject these poor
proposals and stay at the initial point, which the adaptation
tries to improve by decreasing the step size.  If the error
wasn’t due to the HMC integrator but systematic bias from
the ODE integrator then this won’t help and you end up in
a bad state.

And this is all a good outcome compared to what could
potentially happen if not only the gradients were bad but
also the log density calculations were also biased in which
case the acceptance procedure wouldn’t work and you’d
end up with biased chains.  

Personally I’d look at the quality of the data that you’re using.
Misfit can push the parameters into places where the ODE
integrator stumbles.  It’s highly unlikely that adding new
patients will cause the posterior to collapse to pathological
parameter values that the posterior somehow missed before.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
Thanks Mike.

I know this is a constructed exampled which may not be relevant for applications; however, I cannot exclude this from being relevant at this point.

My (user) expectation in this case would be a warning of possibly imprecise gradients and a possibly slightly biased solution. I would be much happier with a result given to me with a warning rather than no result at all. If NUTS could just produce a less accurate, but a still valid result (under the assumption that the truncation error is bias free) - that would be the perfect solution if that's possible.

From what you raised could these workarounds help (or how would they fail):

- Lowering the targeted acceptance rate to 60% or so should allow the Hamiltonian flow to be not that accurate and could solve the issue here, right? Things would not run efficient, but they would run at least.

- How about introducing a minimal step-size? This would limit the acceptance probability whenever that minimal step-size is hit, but again things would keep running, just not as efficient.

- Running things with a fixed step-size, so using vanilla HMC may work as well, right?

On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 1:39:38 AM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
I don’t know what you expect NUTS, or any algorithm, to do.
When the ODE solver starts returning inaccurate gradients
then the Hamiltonian transitions are poor and the acceptance
probability plummets.  All NUTS can do is reject these poor
proposals and stay at the initial point, which the adaptation
tries to improve by decreasing the step size.  If the error
wasn’t due to the HMC integrator but systematic bias from
the ODE integrator then this won’t help and you end up in
a bad state.

And this is all a good outcome compared to what could
potentially happen if not only the gradients were bad but
also the log density calculations were also biased in which
case the acceptance procedure wouldn’t work and you’d
end up with biased chains.  

Personally I’d look at the quality of the data that you’re using.
Misfit can push the parameters into places where the ODE
integrator stumbles.  It’s highly unlikely that adding new
patients will cause the posterior to collapse to pathological
parameter values that the posterior somehow missed before.

That's easy, sure. Going from 1E-10 to 1E-14 for abs and rel tolerances then things work again:

> colMeans(get_sampler_params(fake_run_serial, inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]])
accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__ 
    0.9245461     0.0152286     4.0800000    33.2400000     0.0000000 
     energy__ 
  541.3679865 
> 

So it looks like the limited ODE precision is the problem here. Can I expect NUTS to deal with the limited precision? It obviously doesn't, but I am not sure if increasing the precision is a game I can always play.

I can probably now find again a sample size at which I break things at the fixed 1E-14 precision.

Sebastian

Can you increase accuracy of the ODE integrator to see if that solves
the problem?  Seems like it's an easy enough hypothesis to test, so
to speak.

- Bob

>
> Hi Bob!
>
> Thanks for you answer. You are right in that I was actually referring to posterior std-dev and not MC error.
>
> So I have J patients for which I integrate an ODE. All patients have the exact same parameter set.
>
> For J=6 the posterior std-dev of the parameter of interest is of the order of 1E-2 and the usual sampler parameters look fine:
>

> > colMeans(sp6)
> accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
>    0.90502219    0.02050799    3.60000000   18.52000000    0.00000000
>      energy__
>  407.13425909
>
> Now, when I go to J=8, then I run the same number of iterations, yes (75 warmup and 50 post-warmup), but now things break seriously. The run takes 2H, nothing converges at all and the posterior sd is of the order of 1E-12! The sampler did go completely insane:
>
> > sp8 <- get_sampler_params(res[["8"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> > colMeans(sp8)
> accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
>  1.001197e-01  5.093111e-16  1.000000e+01  1.023000e+03  0.000000e+00
>      energy__
>  1.230724e+03
>
> So the stepsize got reduced to essentially 0, the treedepth is maxed out and we take 1023 leapfrog steps on average.
>
> I think the reason is the limited accuracy of the ODE integrator here which somehow defeats NUTS. I do find this somewhat worrysome, as I thought that a robust numerical procedure should be able to cope with limited precision and simply output a result with limited precision. Anything else I can look into which helps?
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Sunday, February 19, 2017 at 10:38:54 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> MCMC error is estimated as
>
>   posterior std-dev / sqrt(n_eff)
>
> It's not something that gets controlled directly.  Or are you
> talking about the Hamiltonian simulation error due to the leapfrog
> error?  I think that's usually minimal until you hit a divergence and
> it spins off to infinity.
>
> It still gets through as many iterations in the 2H?  Any idea if

>
> - Bob

> > I have encountered the bizarre situation that with increasing the sample size of my fake data simulation the computation time explodes discontinuously at some point and convergence of the parameter estimates vanishes suddenly.
> >

I do so in a very simple way in that there is no between-subject variability and I provide Stan with a lot of data. What happens is when I run this with 4 or 6 patients, then everything is fine (running time is 61s and 75s / estimates are as simulated). Once I go to 8 patients then the running time explodes to 2h and the estimates are just crap.
> >

That is, I provide so much data that the MC error is below the 1E-7 which effectively renders the HMC sampler blind given the precision the data likelihood would provide. However, I would really appreciate an answer in such a situation, but with an artificially more unprecise result - that would be much better than no answer at all.
> >
> > Best,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
For reference: Playing a bit with the adapt_delta parameter indeed works as I expected. That is, reducing adapt_delta to values below the default of 0.9 in rstan made things work again (at the initial precision of 1E-10). Going a bit further showed that when going to even lower adapt_delta of 0.6 results in some nice speedups. The chosen stepsize increases as expected. However, when turning it too low, then things fall apart.

I am aware of the common recommendation to use high adapt_delta values. I wonder if this recommendation still holds when we have to deal with low-precision gradients as it happens when dealing with ODEs where it is super-expensive to get very high precision. The price one will probably pay is not being able to deal with complicated posterior geometry...but nothing is free.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
parts:
The difference is that the HMC error is adjusted with Metropolis.

With bad ODEs, it's not just bad gradients, but also bad solutions.
They're controlled by the same parameter.

We don't know what the cutoff is. Obviously we're using
double-precision (64 bit) floating point in all of our calculations.
But maybe single-precision (32 bit) would be enough. Or maybe
somewhere in between. Double precision is about 1e-14 and
single precision about 1e-7. Unfortunately, those are our only
two viable choices for primitive real types in C++ (until quadruple
precision becomes more common).

What is often more important is the algebra of the expressions,
such as whether subtractions lead to catastrophic cancellations.

I believe most GPUs are only optimized for single-precision, but
I'm not at all certain of that.

- Bob
